title: How Much Can Semiconductor Models Hide?
gist: Advanced packaging forces models to cross company boundaries without exposing proprietary processes, but over-hiding makes predictions break down. The article argues the model's validity envelope and carried uncertainty are as much a deliverable as the model itself, and that winners will turn process knowledge into usable but non-reconstructable models.

insights.claim: Advanced packaging makes supplier-held process behavior affect other companies' parts once assembled, so datasheets, design rules and qualification specs are no longer enough to cross the company boundary.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Value shifts toward firms that can supply predictive, shareable models, not just specs.
insights.quote: The process may still belong to the supplier, but its consequences no longer end at the factory gate.

insights.claim: The core design problem is the 'membrane' between companies: hide too little and the supplier gives away years of process know-how, hide too much and the model loses the behavior and variation the other engineer needs.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Tools that tune this trade-off (obfuscation, normalization, encryption) are the product opportunity for EDA/analytics vendors.
insights.quote: how do you insert a membrane between the companies so they can share a certain amount of data, but not all

insights.claim: Advanced packaging depends on a collaborative supply chain in which dies, substrates, materials and design information come from multiple partners, each owning data for its slice, so no single company necessarily holds the whole history.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Fragmented data ownership is a structural obstacle for OSATs and integrators pursuing digital threads.

insights.claim: ASE's R&D VP argues a connected digital thread does not need full data transparency, only a trusted way to share enough for the next engineering decision.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Signals that large OSATs favor limited-disclosure frameworks over open data sharing.
insights.quote: I don’t think we need complete data transparency to create a connected digital thread

insights.claim: Static datasheet values (CTE, modulus, adhesion, viscosity) capture one moment; properties shift with cure, crosslink density, temperature near Tg and bonding interface, so single fixed inputs cause simulation-to-silicon gaps.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Material suppliers that publish condition-dependent characterization differentiate in packaging design flows.
insights.quote: A digital twin that uses single fixed values for material inputs will always underrepresent real-world risk.

insights.claim: A chiplet's thermal response may suffice for one analysis, yet process variation can change that response in a way the downstream model cannot see.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Thermal sign-off risk in multi-die packages rises when upstream variation is hidden.

insights.claim: Thermal analysis in a package is an integrated problem requiring the whole stack, including substrate and interposer data in a form combinable with the rest of the package.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Supports demand for multiphysics 3D-IC tools from Synopsys and peers.
insights.quote: When you’re talking about thermal, it’s not just the dies

insights.claim: Surrogate models are only as trustworthy as the calibration of the physics models that generated their training data, and calibration needs experimental data that is usually non-proprietary.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Calibration data, not recipe disclosure, is the practical path to credible shareable models.
insights.quote: The surrogate model can be trusted if the simulated data used to create the surrogate model is accurate

insights.claim: Surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within their training region and less reliable when extrapolating, and nothing in the output flags the crossing.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Any AI/surrogate used for packaging sign-off needs explicit validity-domain checks.
insights.quote: surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within the region represented by their training data and less reliable when extrapolating beyond it

insights.claim: Exposing only a few key knobs of a surrogate can preserve proprietary process details, but this only relocates the disclosure problem because the model builder still needs the detailed process recipes.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Model-as-a-service for proprietary processes still requires a trusted party that sees the recipe.
insights.quote: Availability of detailed process recipes is actually the challenge

insights.claim: Synopsys HFSS supports encrypted electromagnetic models so suppliers can share component models without exposing geometry and material information, solving a non-technical hurdle of trade-secret exposure.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Encrypted-model workflows are a sticky feature for EDA vendors serving multi-party packaging.
insights.quote: These encrypted models solve a significant but non-technical hurdle

insights.claim: Encryption protects the recipe but hides where model assumptions stop holding, so a model can be secure and numerically precise yet wrong for the conditions of use.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Model security without validity metadata creates silent engineering risk.
insights.quote: The IP can stay perfectly protected while the engineering decision doesn’t.

insights.claim: A black box needs a visible envelope: the recipe can stay hidden but the conditions defining where the model applies must be exposed.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Expect demand for standards for model validity ranges and provenance.

insights.claim: Synopsys argues uncertainty and validity must travel with each model, including data origin, measurement or calibration method, assumptions, valid range and intended decisions.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Possible basis for interoperability standards in 3D-IC data exchange.
insights.quote: Uncertainty and model validity need to move with the model

insights.claim: When independently built models are joined, differing formats, levels of detail and assumptions (e.g. fixed versus varying temperature) can make each model right alone while the combined package prediction is wrong.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Integration-level validation, not component accuracy, is the bottleneck for heterogeneous packages.
insights.quote: It’s making sure the physical meaning of that data doesn’t get lost along the way.

insights.claim: Proprietary process knowledge may become more valuable in advanced packaging because architectures demand tuned materials, assembly methods and manufacturing windows.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Supports durable pricing power for specialized materials and process suppliers.

insights.claim: The companies that succeed will be those that turn proprietary process knowledge into models others can use without reconstructing the process, not those that share the most.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Pick vendors with model-packaging capability rather than open-data posture.
insights.quote: The recipe can stay private, but the consequences cannot.
